data.title: What Volkswagen Bears Saw Before The Fall
data.description:
If you had looked at Volkswagen on 1 January and decided to wait for clearer signs that its restructuring and EV push were working, you avoided a rough ride. Holding Volkswagen from the start of the year would have meant a 35.2% loss, including dividends. With Q3 2026 showing deeper losses and a tougher backdrop now on display, which assumption from the 2025 bullish or bearish cases could you have questioned more closely at the outset?

Volkswagen has already moved. See which of 210 high quality undervalued stocks still trade below our estimates.

The Two Stories Volkswagen Investors Were Weighing

The shares cost €104 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Volkswagen then faced two very different but credible storylines.

The bullish case saw a Fair Value of €114, a price implied by expectations of 2.8% annual revenue growth and profit margins rising to 4.5%, supported by electrified models, digital services, and restructuring progress.

The bearish view pointed to a Fair Value of €90, tied to slightly declining revenue of 0.5% a year and concern that rising compliance costs and mobility-as-a-service could pressure margins.

What The Results Changed For The Volkswagen Thesis

Volkswagen’s biggest single development was the decision to pursue up to 100,000 job cuts and close several German plants, which backed the bearish concern about heavy restructuring and cost pressure. Q3 2026 then brought deeper losses, with net income moving from a loss of €482 million to a loss of €4.648 billion and net margin sliding to 6.2%. The period therefore supported the cautious case.

The key assumption here was margin repair. For any other manufacturer, it may be useful to question early claims that cost cuts and electrification will quickly lift profitability. Watch reported net margin and restructuring charges together to see whether efficiency plans are actually turning into cleaner earnings.

What Volkswagen’s Fall Asks You To Believe Now

Volkswagen trades at €64.64, after a 35.2% loss from the start of the year. The current price sits below this Narrative’s Fair Value, according to PittTheYounger, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, who focuses on whether tough reforms can reset this industrial giant.

A buyer today would need to believe management follows through on restructuring, restores competitiveness in EVs and holds its ground against Chinese brands in Europe.

"Yet now that the board of Volkswagen has agreed on the tough reforms necessary to turn its fortunes around, the bottom should be in. That doesn't make the shares an outright buy, mind; however, at least the times of profitable short-selling should be over, rendering the OEM a classic hold until the evidence is in that it can prevail against the Chinese onslaught on its home turf."

Another Route Into Auto Reform

Volkswagen’s overhaul raises a simple question. Where else are reforms creating a different kind of earnings mix?

One large automaker is leaning hard into software and connected services. It is not just selling vehicles anymore, but adding recurring digital fees and maintenance revenue.

This business is also nudging commercial fleets toward telematics and energy storage. Customers want uptime, predictable servicing and tools that reduce fuel and repair headaches.

If that shift sticks, more of its value could come from ongoing subscriptions and support rather than one off metal sales.
